name: Compression undershirt

lead: A compression undershirt is a close-fitting elastic top, often worn under a shirt, that firms the torso outline.

It is used for a smoother silhouette under fitted clothing. The sports-performance literature on compression garments is separate and shows little performance effect, while the visual smoothing is immediate.

paras: Elastic fabric applies gentle pressure to flatten and redistribute soft tissue, giving a more even surface under clothes.
Tight garments can be hot and uncomfortable, and overly restrictive ones may limit breathing or movement. The effect is cosmetic and present only while worn.

lead: A compression undershirt is a close-fitting elastic top worn beneath other clothing. In appearance discussions it is used to give the torso a smoother, firmer outline under fitted shirts. It belongs to the broader family of compression garments, which Grokipedia describes as elastic clothing engineered to apply mechanical pressure to the body, with medical, athletic and cosmetic variants, the last including shapewear and girdles.[1]

Most published research on compression garments concerns medical uses such as venous insufficiency and lymphedema, or sports recovery, and does not address cosmetic torso smoothing. The few human studies that involve compression shirts specifically test posture, and found no significant change in head or shoulder angles in one trial of healthy men.[2]
infobox: Consumer clothing; medical compression hosiery is separately classified

paras: Compression garments are made from elastomeric fibres and applied pressure is quantified in millimetres of mercury. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, says medical stockings used for varicose veins or after surgery are often in the 20-50 mmHg range, and that athletic garments are typically in a lower comfort range, though it presents these figures without independent verification here.[1]

Undershirts sold for appearance are generally closer to the cosmetic and athletic categories than the medical one. Product designs vary from plain fitted shirts to versions with panels or straps intended to cue posture.

Grokipedia traces compression techniques to ancient bandaging, citing the Corpus Hippocraticum and an Egyptian papyrus, and elastic stockings to nineteenth-century England, with later growth in athletic and cosmetic garments.[1] No source examined documents when compression undershirts specifically entered men's style or looksmaxxing discussion.

Medical compression is described as working by squeezing superficial veins and limiting fluid filtration in tissue, which can help venous return and reduce swelling in the limbs.[1] Cosmetic compression garments are said by sellers to apply gentle pressure that flattens and redistributes soft tissue, producing a more even surface beneath clothing. This visual-smoothing mechanism has not been measured in published studies.

The smoothing effect is immediate and exists only while the garment is worn. Published trials have tested other outcomes, mainly posture, and are summarised under Clinical studies. Sports-performance research on compression garments is a separate literature and is not specific to cosmetic use.

Grokipedia reports that garments that are too tight can cause pressure injury, reduced blood supply or dermatitis in medical contexts, while too-loose ones provide little compression.[1] For torso garments worn for appearance, comfort and heat retention are the usual practical concerns, and overly restrictive designs can limit movement or breathing. These points reflect general guidance rather than trials of cosmetic undershirts.

In style communities, compression undershirts are mentioned as a low-cost way to present a tidier torso under fitted clothing; the wiki's summary describes an instant smoother silhouette. These are community characterisations of appearance, and they have not been tested.
No studies were found that test compression undershirts for torso appearance. Several small trials have used compression shirts as a comparison or base garment in posture research.

A randomised crossover study in the Journal of Manipulative and Physiological Therapeutics had 30 healthy men complete three 15-minute laptop writing tasks wearing a posture-cueing shirt, a compression shirt or no shirt. Head and shoulder angles did not differ significantly between conditions, and pain ratings were lower with the posture-cueing shirt than with no shirt but not lower than with the compression shirt.[2]

A randomised trial in the Journal of Athletic Training enrolled 38 overhead athletes with rounded-shoulder posture, who wore a compression shirt either with or without tensioned straps, and measured posture and scapular muscle activity with and without the brace.[3] A 2024 study in the Journal of Dance Medicine and Science compared a compression jacket with elastic bands against a control compression shirt in 15 dance students and reported on trunk-pelvic angle reproduction.[4] These studies address posture and proprioception rather than appearance, and they involved small samples.
